1.pericope_label: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him. When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born. And they said unto him, In Bethlehem of Judea: for thus it is written by the prophet, And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the date by the king's death rather than the birth, setting it just before a Passover in a year answering to four before the common era, and concludes that our ordinary reckoning is wrong and the Nativity earlier than the numbering suggests; on the season he says only that flocks in the open field point to spring rather than winter. He also supplies the timing of the reign, an old rule drawing to its blood-stained close and the eldest son under condemnation as the history opens, and points out that the Evangelist is not quoting the prophet himself but recording how the scribes quoted him, which is why the words follow neither the Greek version nor the Hebrew closely. Robertson thinks the phrase about the east goes with the seeing rather than the star, so that they saw it at its rising; he recalls what anyone who knows Josephus will remember of the king, a man who had put to death two sons by his best-loved wife, that wife herself, another son once his heir, and her brother and mother; and he doubts whether a formal council was called at all, since the question could as easily have been put to one leader after another. Lightfoot enters a caution about a story often repeated, that this king is said by very many authors to have slain the Sanhedrim, which he holds must not be understood of the whole body nor taken for its abolition.

Calvin draws a larger inference from the form of the quotation, that Matthew thought it enough to indicate the passage and followed the ordinary reading because he wrote in Greek, which tells against the notion that this Gospel was composed in Hebrew.
Henry marks the obscurity as deliberate, that one who was the desire of all nations came into the world unregarded, having emptied himself and made himself of no reputation.

Chrysostom argues that the star was manifestly not one of the common stars, since none moves as this did, from east to south, which is the lie of Palestine with respect to Persia; and he turns the astrological reading around, since the art is used not to learn a birth from the stars but to forecast a life from its hour, whereas these men did the converse. On the prophecy he presses the wording, that it does not say the ruler shall be in Bethlehem but shall come out of it, which shows he was only to be born there.

Gregory names the party he argues with, heretics who hold every man born under the aspect of some planet and cite this very text for it; far be it, he answers, from the hearts of the faithful to call anything fate, since prayer is vain for men who live by it, and providence is banished along with piety when man is made the instrument of the motions of the sky. He adds that when heavenly greatness shows itself earthly greatness is confounded. Leo addresses the troubled king directly: his alarm is groundless, since his nature cannot contain Christ and the Lord of the world is not content with the narrow bounds of one dominion. Augustine sets the parties against each other in a sentence, that the Magi seek a Redeemer while Herod fears a successor, and asks what the tribunal of the Judge will do if the cradle already makes proud kings tremble; he also notices what the star did not do, since it could have conducted them straight to the town and instead vanished until the Jews themselves had named the place.

debates.question: What was the star that the Magi saw?

positions.position: Manifestly not a common star, since none of them moves from east to south as this did
Not a fate: the text must not be surrendered to those who make every man born under a planet
A servant, advancing slowly to minister and vanishing when the Jews had named the place
A question of phrasing rather than astronomy: they saw it at its rising, not in the eastern sky

outliers.claim: Infers from the free form of the quotation, which follows the ordinary Greek reading, that this Gospel was not composed in Hebrew.
Cautions against the often-repeated story that this king slew the Sanhedrim, which he holds must not be understood of the whole body nor taken for its abolition.

7.pericope_label: Then Herod, when he had privily called the wise men, enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also. When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh. And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the secrecy true to the king's nature, a man probably himself a believer in astrology and haunted by what the star portended, whose next move is to measure his danger; he corrects the English too, since the question is not when the star appeared but when the star now visible had first done so, and on the gifts he compares the presents Jacob sent into Egypt and notes that the word for treasures means the caskets they were carried in. Robertson notes that the Sanhedrin had not been told why the birthplace mattered, so the motive is hidden from the Magi too, says the deceit was plausible enough to have worked but for the intervention that followed, and agrees that the star guided them not to the town but to the place within it. Barnes notes that the errand would have looked suspicious had it not been clothed in religion, and that the king had asked the exact time, reckoning the star had appeared at the birth; with Clarke he takes the star for a luminous meteor at no great height, since it could not otherwise have marked the particular house. Lightfoot supposes it shone on the birth night and then disappeared, no guide being needed to a city as well known as Jerusalem, and reappeared for the road to Bethlehem.

Calvin supplies the politics, that the tyrant dared not avow his fear lest it give fresh courage to a people he knew hated him; and he is indignant at who did not go, calling it base sluggishness that not one Jew offered himself as escort to these foreigners, the scribes naming the place and then letting them depart alone, not a man moving a step.

Clarke calls the pretended homage exquisite hypocrisy, since the man wished only to find the child in order to murder him, and observes how the God who searches the heart defeats such designs; on the gifts he observes that in the east nobody approaches a king empty-handed, and reports without adopting the reading that makes the three stand for divinity, royal office and manhood. Wesley alone asks what the gifts were for, calling them a most seasonable and providential assistance toward a long and expensive journey into Egypt.

Chrysostom catches what the king's wording gives away, that he says the young child and not the king, grudging him the title; he names two heretics and tells them to blush, since the swaddling clothes and the stall prove the flesh while the gifts prove that the worship was not offered to a mere man; and he praises the Magi's obedience, that they did not ask what need there was of flight if this child were really some great one, true faith asking no reason for a command.

Augustine describes the star's movement as service rather than mechanism: it advanced slowly to do its duty, ministering to the Lord and not ruling his fate, and its light filled the lodging before it went out. Gregory gives the symbolic reading of the gifts, gold to a king, frankincense in sacrifice to God, myrrh for embalming, and turns each into a duty, incense standing for prayer and myrrh for mortification; the detour home he makes an allegory of the return to Paradise, forbidden by the road we left it on. Leo observes that the child was in stature an infant, needing help and unable to speak and in nothing different from other children, so witnesses of this kind ought to have settled that the eternal Son had taken a true human nature.

debates.question: What did the gifts of the Magi mean?

positions.position: Ordinary eastern custom, since nobody approaches a king empty-handed
Gold to a king, frankincense in sacrifice to God, myrrh for embalming, each also standing for a duty
Proof that the worship was not offered to a mere man, as the swaddling clothes prove the flesh
Provision for the journey into Egypt that was about to be required

outliers.claim: Is indignant at who did not go, calling it base sluggishness that the scribes named the place and then let the foreigners depart alone, not a man moving a step.
Alone asks what the gifts were for, and calls them a most seasonable and providential assistance toward a long and expensive journey into Egypt.

13.pericope_label: And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him. When he arose, he took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt: And was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.

schools.summary: Barnes puts Egypt some sixty miles off, a Roman province where Greek was spoken and where there were Jews enough to have a temple and synagogues, so that Joseph would be among his own countrymen and still beyond the reach of Herod's jurisdiction. Lightfoot fills in how those Jews came to be there, some from the old flight under Jeremiah and many more drawn later by the temple built at Heliopolis. Ellicott says the nearness of the country had always made it the natural refuge, and makes two observations about the telling: the phrase naming the child before the mother he calls significantly reverential, since in an ordinary narrative the natural order would have been the wife and then the child, and he finds in the sheer brevity of the account an argument, so far as it goes, against treating the story as myth; on the chronology he notes that the king died a little before a Passover, so the stay in Egypt can have been only a few months. Robertson says only that the evangelist quotes the prophet to show the application.

Calvin calls the method itself remarkable, that God chose to preserve his Son by flight, and supposes the order was delayed until the mother had recovered enough from childbirth to travel; on the quotation he attacks a rival reading rather than the difficulty, saying that those who make the prophet mean something else grievously pervert his words, whose design was to establish a charge.

Clarke states the difficulty of the quotation without softening it: the words in their place refer to the deliverance of Israel and to nothing else, and his own suggestion is that so extraordinary a deliverance had passed into a proverb for any signal rescue; beyond that, he confesses he can see no other reference the words can have to the case in hand. He also notes that Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt had the advantage of the older Greek version to hand. Wesley solves the same difficulty by the grammar, holding that the word rendered as purpose frequently signifies not the design of an action but merely its consequence, so that what is meant is that the saying was fulfilled anew, Christ being the Son of God in a far higher sense than Israel was.

Henry notices the irony of the timing, that the flight is the direct result of the visit paid to the child, since until then the obscurity he lay in had been his protection; the little respect shown him in infancy did not honour him among his people but only exposed him.

Chrysostom turns the same fact into consolation, that the tyrant rages against him from the moment of his birth and the mother is driven into a foreign country, so that a man who meets trouble at the beginning of his own spiritual course need not be discouraged but may bear it with this example before him. On the prophecy he states the principle broadly, that it is a law of prophecy for things to be said in one place of one subject and fulfilled in another of a different one.

Augustine refuses to let the flight be merely an escape and sets it against the older history: Moses had shut the light of day away from the Egyptians, and Christ by going down brought light back to those sitting in darkness, so that he fled in order to enlighten them and not in order to evade his enemies. Bede takes it as precedent rather than symbol, that the elect are often driven from their homes by the wickedness of others, and that the man who afterwards told his followers to flee from one city to another had first done himself what he enjoined.

debates.question: How does a prophecy about Israel apply to Christ?

positions.position: It does not, strictly: the words refer to Israel's deliverance only, and had probably passed into a proverb for any signal rescue
By grammar: the word for purpose often means only consequence, so the saying was fulfilled anew in a higher sense
By a law of prophecy, whereby things are said in one place of one subject and fulfilled in another of a different one
Those who make the prophet mean something else pervert his words, whose design was to establish a charge

debates.question: Why was the flight into Egypt of all places?

positions.position: Because it was near, a Roman province with Greek spoken and Jews enough for a temple and synagogues, beyond Herod's reach
So that he who had shut the light from the Egyptians under Moses might bring it back to them
To set the precedent he afterwards enjoined, of fleeing from one city to another under persecution

outliers.claim: Calls the phrase naming the child before the mother significantly reverential, since an ordinary narrative would have said the wife and then the child, and finds in the account's brevity an argument against treating it as myth.
Confesses he can see no reference the quoted words can have to the case in hand beyond their having passed into a proverb for any signal deliverance.

When he arose, he took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt:

16.pericope_label: Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

schools.summary: Barnes points out that the word does not mean the Magi set out to deride the king, only that he was disappointed by their not returning, and that he had expected to send one executioner against one child; with Clarke he supplies the history behind the lament, the captives gathered at Ramah after the city fell. Robertson explains the width of the order, that Herod had no way of knowing the child's age and therefore took in every boy rather than risk the one. Ellicott states the objection to the massacre plainly, that neither Josephus nor any other writer mentions it and its historicity has been questioned on that ground, and answers that it is admitted on all hands to be entirely in keeping with the man's character, a king tormented by incurable disease and still more incurable suspicion; the lament he anchors to the ground itself, since the tomb of Rachel stood on the road to the very town where the children died. Lightfoot uses the age limit to date the episode, reckoning about two years since the star had shone, and explains why the family had stayed so long in one small town, supposing that a Messiah born there was to be brought up nowhere else.

Calvin puts the king's grievance more sharply than the others, that the evangelist reports what the man felt rather than what was true: he believed himself deceived by men who had merely refused to share his cruelty, and was in fact caught by his own trick, the pretence that he too meant to pay homage. He notes the silence of the historians and names the one writer he knows who alludes to the massacre; and on the lament he identifies what it originally described, the destruction of the tribe of Benjamin in the prophet's own day, calling the device by its name, a personification that puts the mourning into the mouth of Rachel and has great power in moving the affections.

Clarke gives the one classical allusion to the massacre, from a Latin author of the fourth century, who reports the jest that it was better to be this king's pig than his son; and he adds that Bethlehem at this hour resembled Ramah, weeping for children slaughtered as the other had wept for children carried away. Wesley says the king's pride made him read the Magi's departure as designed to expose him to the derision of his subjects, and works out the figure of the lament, that the people of Ramah were descended from Rachel and that she is represented as risen from her grave to bewail them, the closing words meaning simply that they are dead.
Henry describes the waiting before the rage, a king hoping that visitors slow to return would still be sure, and growing suspicious that they had gone over to the new king's interest.

Chrysostom will not call the state of mind anger, since the case called for fear and awe and the man ought to have seen he was attempting the impossible; but a soul past cure yields to none of the medicines God gives.

Augustine observes that in persecuting Christ the king unintentionally furnished an army of martyrs of the Lord's own age, and that this enemy could never have profited the children by his love as he did by his hate. Bede takes them for a figure of all Christ's martyrs and presses the details, that their infancy shows the glory of martyrdom reached by humility alone, and that their dying in Bethlehem and its borders foreshadows persecution both where the Church began and throughout the world.

debates.question: How should the silence of the historians about the massacre be met?

positions.position: By character: it is admitted on all hands to be entirely in keeping with a king tormented by incurable disease and still more incurable suspicion
By noting that one writer does allude to it, though Josephus does not
By producing that allusion, with its jest that it was better to be the king's pig than his son

outliers.claim: Turns the massacre into a gain, since in persecuting Christ the king unintentionally furnished an army of martyrs of the Lord's own age, and could never have profited the children by his love as he did by his hate.
Names the device in the lament, a personification that puts the mourning into the mouth of a woman long dead and has great power in moving the affections.

19.pericope_label: But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeareth in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, Saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child’s life. And he arose, and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding, being warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee: And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene.

schools.summary: Barnes supposes a second person genuinely meant in the plural of the message, the king's eldest son having been put to death by his father a few days before his own; he gives the character of the new ruler, a temper as cruel as his father's, three thousand men put to death at a single Passover, and banishment after nine years, and supplies the fact that gives the closing name its edge, that the town itself was proverbial for wickedness. Ellicott allows that others may have been implicated in the plural, but thinks the phrasing likelier suggested by the parallel words spoken to Moses; he also corrects the title of the new ruler, since this prince was never recognised as king by the emperor but held the lesser rank of ethnarch, the higher word surviving only in popular use. Robertson agrees about the plural and puts it as a habit of speech, a general statement covering a particular fact; he adds what makes the fear intelligible, that in a fit of temper before his death the old king had altered his will again and put the worst of his surviving sons in the place meant for another; and on the last quotation he states the problem exactly, that the evangelist writes prophets in the plural and no single prophecy says the Messiah should be called by this name, suggesting that the term of contempt is what is meant and that several prophecies are combined. Lightfoot grants that the two passages usually offered both have their weight and will dismiss neither, but takes the evangelist to be speaking of the outward and mean condition of the Saviour.

Calvin reads the interval abroad as a test passed, that Joseph kept his feet firm there until a command recalled him, and takes it for evidence that the Lord never disappoints his own but sends help in season. On the last quotation he will not have the passage about the branch treated as an etymology at all, holding that the evangelist is making an allusion and not deriving one word from another.

Clarke sets out the division of the kingdom under the will, Galilee and the country beyond Jordan to one son, the northern tetrarchy to another, Judea to the eldest then living, and adds that the son who had died had cleared his way to the throne by procuring the deaths of his elder brothers. On the last quotation he admits he cannot tell which prophets are intended, and reports the two passages usually offered, the promise about the Nazarite at Samson's birth and the branch from the stem of Jesse. Wesley puts the same difficulty as a distinction, that the thing was spoken in effect by several of the prophets though in express words by none, and that to be called by this name is to be despised and rejected.

Henry states the principle behind the return in a sentence: Egypt may serve to sojourn in or shelter in for a while but not to abide in, and one sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel must go back to them.

Bede makes the sequence a figure, the slaughter, the persecutor's death soon after and the return together showing that persecutions against the Church end in the death of the persecutor, the restoring of peace, and the return of saints who had hidden themselves. Augustine raises the difficulty the fear of the new ruler creates: if the family avoided Judea on his account, how could they go up to Jerusalem every year of the childhood, as another Gospel relates? A festival crowd would hide them, he answers, and a short stay end the risk, so they could keep the feast without living where they dared not live.

debates.question: Where is it written that he should be called a Nazarene?

positions.position: Nowhere in the singular: the plural is used and several prophecies are being combined, the term of contempt being what is meant
Spoken in effect by several prophets though in express words by none, the name meaning despised and rejected
Undecidable: the two passages usually offered are the Nazarite at Samson's birth and the branch from the stem of Jesse
Both passages have weight, but the evangelist is speaking of the outward and mean condition of the Saviour
Not an etymology at all, but an allusion; the evangelist is not deriving one word from another

debates.question: Why is the plural used when only one man had been named?

positions.position: Because a second person is genuinely meant, the eldest son having been executed days before his father
Because the phrasing echoes the words spoken to Moses, though others may also have been implicated
Because it is a habit of speech, a general statement covering a particular fact

outliers.claim: Harmonises the fear of Archelaus with the yearly visits to Jerusalem, since a festival crowd would hide the family and a short stay end the risk.
Supplies the fact that gives the closing name its edge, that the town itself was proverbial for wickedness.
